A2.text:
Gunel's sister, Leyla, was getting married. She was engaged to Elvin for one year, and now they wanted to tie the knot. The wedding was in a big restaurant in Baku. There were three hundred guests.

Gunel's little son, Ali, had an important job. He was six, and he had to carry the rings to the bride and groom.

Everybody wanted the day to go off without a hitch. But Ali was excited. He ran around the restaurant with the small box.

At the ceremony, the music started. Ali walked to Leyla and Elvin. He opened the box. It was empty!

The guests were quiet. Leyla looked at Gunel. Gunel looked at Ali. “Where are the rings?” she whispered. Ali started to cry.

Then Grandfather Ismayil stood up. This day was also his anniversary. Fifty years ago, he married Grandmother Sara. He took off his old gold ring, and Sara took off hers.

“Take our rings,” Grandfather said. “It is a family tradition now.”

Everybody clapped. Leyla and Elvin got married with the old rings. Later, a waiter found the new rings under a table.

In the evening, Grandfather made a toast. “To fifty years of love!” Everybody cheered. The bride was beautiful, but nobody could steal the show from Grandfather and Grandmother.

B1.text:
Leyla and Elvin had been engaged for a year, and by June they were ready to tie the knot. Their wedding was planned for three hundred guests at a restaurant on the Baku seafront, and Leyla's sister Gunel had spent months making sure everything would go off without a hitch.

One small but important job was given to Gunel's six-year-old son, Ali. He would walk down the aisle in a tiny suit and bring the rings to the bride and groom.

Ali took the responsibility very seriously — for about ten minutes. After that, he was running between tables, showing the velvet box to every guest who would look.

When the ceremony began, the room went dark except for the lights on the couple. The music changed, and Ali walked proudly towards them. Elvin smiled, took the box and opened it.

It was empty.

Three hundred people held their breath. Leyla's face turned white. Gunel was already on her knees, searching Ali's pockets while he burst into tears.

Then Leyla's grandfather Ismayil slowly stood up. That very day, by pure coincidence, was his fiftieth wedding anniversary. He pulled a thin, worn gold ring off his finger and turned to his wife. Grandmother Sara understood at once and took off hers.

“We've worn these for fifty years,” he said, placing them in Elvin's hand. “I think they still have a little luck in them. Let's call it a new tradition.”

The applause was so loud the DJ had to turn the music down. Leyla and Elvin exchanged the old rings, and both of them were crying. Half an hour later, a waiter found the new rings under table fourteen, where Ali had been showing them to his cousins.

Later that night, Grandfather Ismayil raised his glass for a toast. “To the next fifty years,” he said, “and to grandsons who make sure nobody forgets a wedding.”

The bride looked beautiful and the groom looked happy, but everyone agreed: the grandparents had stolen the show.

B2.text:
After a year of being engaged, Leyla and Elvin were ready to tie the knot, and Leyla's elder sister Gunel had appointed herself commander-in-chief of the operation. For four months she had controlled every variable — three hundred guests, a seafront restaurant, a seating plan negotiated with the delicacy of a peace treaty — so that the day would go off without a hitch.

Her single concession to chaos was her six-year-old son, Ali, who had been entrusted with carrying the rings to the bride and groom. He accepted the role with tremendous solemnity, which lasted for roughly ten minutes. Thereafter he was seen sprinting between tables, displaying the velvet box to any guest who showed the faintest interest.

When the ceremony began, the lights dimmed to a single spotlight on the couple. The music swelled, Ali advanced with immense dignity, and Elvin, smiling, opened the box.

It was empty.

Three hundred people stopped breathing simultaneously. Leyla went the colour of her dress. Gunel was already on her knees, turning out Ali's pockets while he dissolved into tears.

It was at this moment that Leyla's grandfather Ismayil rose slowly to his feet. That day, by sheer coincidence, marked his fiftieth wedding anniversary. He worked a thin gold ring, worn almost smooth, off his finger and turned to his wife. Grandmother Sara needed no explanation; she was already removing her own.

“We've worn these for half a century,” he said, pressing them into Elvin's palm. “There may be a little luck left in them yet. Let's consider it a new family tradition.”

The ovation was so loud the DJ was obliged to lower the music. The couple exchanged the old rings with tears streaming down their faces. Half an hour later, a waiter retrieved the missing pair from beneath table fourteen, where Ali had apparently been conducting a private viewing for his cousins.

Towards midnight, Grandfather Ismayil stood to propose a toast. “To the next fifty years,” he declared, “and to grandsons who guarantee that no one will ever forget a wedding.”

The bride was radiant and the groom visibly overjoyed, yet when guests later described the evening, they all said the same thing: the grandparents had completely stolen the show.

podcast.title: Five hundred guests

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: How big is a wedding in your country? Guess: how many guests were at the wedding Sam went to?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is weddings. And I have big news: last Saturday I went to my first Azerbaijani wedding!
My cousin's wedding! Tell everyone how many guests there were.
Five hundred! In England, a big wedding is maybe a hundred people.
[laugh] Five hundred is normal here. Cousins, neighbours, colleagues, neighbours of colleagues…
And the dancing! Four hours of dancing. My legs hurt more than after a long run.
What did you think of the bride and groom?
They looked so happy. But the ceremony was short — the party was the main event.
That's a tradition here. The official part is often a few days before, just with the family.
And someone gave a toast every ten minutes!
Did you give one?
I did! In Azerbaijani. Three sentences. Everyone clapped — I think because they were surprised.
[chuckle] They loved it. But you know who can always steal the show?
Aysu! She danced with the groom's grandfather!
For twenty minutes! Now, what about weddings in England?
My sister just got engaged. She and her boyfriend want a small wedding — forty guests, in a garden.
Forty! My mum would say that is just the family. When will they tie the knot?
Next summer. And I'm going to give the toast — in English this time. [laugh]
Will you bring the Azerbaijani dancing to England?
Definitely. Forty English people dancing for four hours — they won't know what hit them.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is a typical wedding like in your country — big or small?
And what's the best wedding you've ever been to? See you next time!
Bye for now!
